member of the commission. mr president, the community and the republic of gabon have negotiated and initialled, on 28 october 2005, a fisheries partnership agreement for a period of six years. the new protocol has been in provisional application since december 2005 under a decision of the council. on the date of its entry into force, this agreement will repeal and replace the agreement between the european economic community and the republic of gabon on fishing off the coast of gabon, which entered into force in december 1998. the financial contribution is fixed at eur 860 000 per year. of this financial contribution, 60% will allow annual financial support for defining and implementing a sectoral fisheries policy in gabon, with a view to introducing responsible and sustainable fishing. this new protocol provides fishing possibilities for 24 tuna seiners and 16 surface long-liners, with an annual reference tonnage of 11 000 tonnes. the agreement is part of an important network of ec tuna agreements in the atlantic ocean off the western african coast. the commission considers that the agreement will give the community and gabon an appropriate legal and political framework for monitoring and controlling the activities of the eu fleet in the gabonese fishing area. it also allows the community to support the development of the sector in this country, for the mutual benefit of the parties.
the rapporteur. mr president, the european union and the republic of gabon negotiated and signed on 28 october 2005 a multiannual fisheries partnership covering european fisheries relations with the republic of gabon. the partnership agreement, which is accompanied by a protocol, has a duration of six years, while the technical and financial conditions for fishing activities have already started on 3 december 2005. the main objective of the partnership agreement, which goes beyond the narrow commercial framework of the previous bilateral agreement, is to develop a sustainable fisheries policy with responsible exploitation of fisheries resources, to strengthen coastal populations, to create small local freezing and processing industries through more general economic and scientific cooperation. the monitoring of fishing vessels by satellite is an important innovation in the fight against illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing. as the commissioner responsible for fisheries, mr borg, pointed out, this new agreement opens a new chapter in cooperation between the european union and the gabonese republic, as it will intensify its efforts to ensure the sustainability of fisheries in its waters. it should be stressed that agreements of this kind are particularly important as they promote economic development and cooperation with third countries. the agreement with gabon on fisheries is another development tool used by the european union to highlight its solidarity and willingness to cooperate further with developing third countries. i therefore believe that it is necessary to inform the european parliament in good time, as the body directly elected by the citizens, and not to call it a year later simply to ratify the decisions.

member of the commission. undertakings that are active in the processing and marketing of agricultural products listed in annex 1 to the treaty may be granted ‘de minimis’ aid of up to eur 200 000 over a period of three fiscal years, provided of course that a series of conditions are fulfilled. before 1 january 2007, the ‘de minimis’ aid for processing and for marketing was governed by the provisions of commission regulation (ec) no 1860/2004 and limited to eur 3000 per beneficiary over any period of three years, within a maximum global ceiling established for each member state. processing and marketing of agricultural products have been included within the scope of the new regulatory framework because of the similarities between those activities on the one hand and processing and marketing of non-agricultural products, on the other. in the field of processing and marketing of agricultural products, ‘de minimis’ aid may be accumulated with state aid, provided that this does not exceed the maximum aid intensity laid down for measures supported by state aid. with the new and much more flexible rules for the ‘de minimis’ regulations, greece, like all other member states, will have more scope for granting aid in a much more rapid way, as the ‘de minimis’ aid will not have to be notified. there will be more advantageous conditions than those laid down in other rules applicable to state aid. this flexibility will enhance the development of the agricultural sector in member states within the european union.

in writing. the gue/ngl group welcomes all agreements that promote bilateral travel arrangements between the eu and the russian federation. these facilitate the travelling of russian citizens to the eu and vice versa. moreover, such arrangements are considered to be an important step forward, aiming at establishing better communication ties and creating political dialogue on a cultural, economical and political level. however the gue/ngl group is very much concerned about the ec-russia short-stay visa agreement because of its close political link to the ec-russia readmission agreement, which seriously undermines the protection and rights of refugees and immigrants, as well as their fundamental rights. the gue/ngl group is also strongly opposed to article 11 of the joint declaration to the agreement which defines "biometric identifiers" in diplomatic passports as a priority for ensuring a high level of document security. gue/ngl is also opposed to the fact that certain provisions of the agreement apply exclusively to certain categories or groups of people. this is considered discriminatory and the gue/ngl group stresses that the facilitation procedure for access visas should apply and be guaranteed equally to all citizens of the eu member states and citizens of the russian federation.

member of the commission. mr president, madam member, ladies and gentlemen, allow me to thank the committee on legal affairs and the rapporteur, mrs lévai, for the draft report on the commission recommendation of 18 october 2005 on the collective management of copyright and related rights across borders for legal online music services. i would like to emphasise that the commission's recommendations were initially motivated by the concerns of the authors. authors, composers and music publishers have informed the commission that they do not receive any income from the online exploitation of their works. however, our analysis has made it increasingly clear that managing the use of protected works online by territory is too complex, especially in the digital environment. given the complex relationships between collective management organisations that manage the same rights separately in each territory, it appears that revenues do not reach authors or other rightholders. the commission's recommendation therefore aims to ensure that authors, composers and music publishers receive a fair share of online revenues. we also believe that the licensing system can be improved to facilitate the development of new online services while protecting and genuinely promoting the interests of rights holders. to be clear, the recommendation does not represent a specific licensing model, but introduces the principle that rightholders should be free to choose the most appropriate and efficient online rights manager or licensing platform for the management of their online rights. it also aims to ensure that those rightholders generate income from the online exploitation of their musical works. this will ensure that the value of the works of rightholders is fully protected. this is not a race to the bottom, downward. this focus on the interests of rightholders is also reflected in the provisions of the recommendation concerning the governance of transparency, dispute resolution, the liability of rightholders and the fair and balanced representation of all categories of rightholders on the boards of collective management organisations. the commission welcomes the strong support for this draft report from parliament. while we are still monitoring the impact of the recommendations and seeking stakeholder input in this area, it is already apparent that several initiatives have been launched to strengthen governance. for example, in 2006, the world music publishers' trade association and the umbrella organisation of european collective management societies adopted a joint declaration setting out agreed rules for online rights management. various rightholders, including smaller collective management organisations and publishers, have expressed enthusiasm for the business opportunities offered by the recommendation on online music services. the commission sees the licensing of online services for the whole of the european union as an opportunity to promote the value of music and thus to promote different cultures and their musical works across the eu. the creation of new markets for specific music genres and the finding of a genuine online audience will undoubtedly contribute to the promotion of european cultural diversity. e draft report calls on the commission to submit a proposal for a directive on this issue. however, the commission would like to note that the online market is still developing and we must be particularly careful not to limit its potential by taking an overly rigid approach. and, as i said, we are only now examining the situation in the period after the recommendation was adopted. however, i can assure members that our aim is to ensure that rights holders receive the revenue from their creative activity and that rights users have the necessary licences, in a simple and straightforward way. we believe that this is a crucial issue if we are to promote and maintain europe's cultural diversity. the commission will of course keep parliament informed of this.

least one third of children under three years of age should have access to care. this objective was taken up in the european employment strategy in 2003 and reaffirmed in the integrated guidelines for growth and jobs (2005-08). there are countries where these quotas are already being exceeded - in some cases by a considerable amount. for the offers for children under 3 years of age, there are about seven member states which meet or exceed the targeted quota of 33%. the other countries are below this and some of them have a very low supply. similarly, the shares of member states above and below the barcelona target of 90% for children from three years of age up to the age of school entry are very high. this means that many member states will have to significantly step up their efforts to achieve the barcelona objectives. the joint employment report 2006/2007, which the council adopted a few weeks ago, on 22 february, addresses this point by unequivocally criticising the slow progress at least 60% of the eu average. it is therefore of paramount importance that the european council of 8 and 9 march endorsed the european alliance for families. this alliance will give new impetus to the implementation of the agreed targets on childcare and women's employment. this alliance will also be the subject of the epsco council discussions on 30 may this year. the european alliance for families aims to improve family-friendly living conditions in the european union. it will provide a platform for the exchange of views and information between member states. it is closely linked to the actual implementation of equality, as improved family and work-life balance leads to greater equality of opportunity in working life. expertise also shows: if we consistently go our way, creating better conditions for young parents, expanding childcare and early education, systematically developing family-oriented work structures with the economy, we will have a positive impact precisely in the period that is particularly difficult demographically and economically, namely the period from 2020 to 2030. the question of reconciling family and work is not just a matter for the state, but also for the economy. children are our future - they are the workers, the consumers, but also the parents of tomorrow. the need to take account of the needs of families must be part of the company's strategy and culture. flexible working hours and parttime models for both mothers and fathers should then be standard across the board. it would be helpful if companies were to recognise that it is also economically viable to take account of the needs of families. because only mothers and fathers who know that their children are well looked after during the day can concentrate fully on their work. the state and the social security institutions also benefit from a family-friendly attitude in the enterprises: the more mothers and fathers are able to participate in working life, the more taxes and social contributions are paid. but i also want to make sure that we do not lose sight of the children when we look at the state and the economy. their welfare should be the focus of europe. vice-president of the commission. i have to say, madam president, the commission is aware that counterfeiting of medicines - as the honourable member has pointed out - is a global problem and can have serious health consequences. we are therefore following this problem very closely and i cannot fail to tell you that i am extremely concerned about it. the commission has developed a general strategy against the counterfeiting of medicines in the european union and, in view of the international dimension of the problem, has ensured that it is linked to and complements the activities of international partners, such as the world health organisation and the council of europe. the community legal framework allowing the authorities to detain counterfeit medicinal products introduced into or found on the community market consists of community legislation on medicinal products, on the conduct of customs authorities and on the enforcement of intellectual property rights. the main responsibility for enforcing the existing rules lies with the member states. over the past five years, member states have detected 27 cases of falsified medicines in the legal supply chain and 170 cases in the illegal supply chain on the eu market. this may not seem like a huge number, but the seizure of counterfeit medicines by customs at external borders also indicates a significant increase in recent years. statistics for 2005 show that customs at the eu's external borders seized 560 000 counterfeit medicines. a first analysis of member states' 2006 figures has shown that in 2006 more than 1.5 million counterfeit medicines were estimated to have been seized by customs. that's a dramatic increase. in its communication to the council, the european parliament and the economic and social committee on a customs response to recent developments in counterfeiting and piracy, the commission presented an action plan containing a series of concrete measures to combat this increase. two of the most important measures have already been taken: the creation of an electronic system for the rapid exchange of risk information on novel counterfeits between customs authorities and the establishment of a system for companies to provide customs authorities with information on counterfeits needed for countermeasures. in addition, in march 2006, the commission issued a warning against the sale of counterfeit medicines on the internet in order to raise public awareness of the problem. in this warning, the commission publicly announced that it would analyse the situation as part of a project and, in cooperation with the member states, the european medicines agency and international partners, examine whether intervention was necessary to protect public health. the project will, inter alia, deal with the trafficking of counterfeit medicines via the internet. the commission will build on this analysis, which has already begun, and develop policy solutions to close any gaps in the legislation. if necessary, we will have to amend european pharmaceutical legislation. these solutions will of course be based on impact assessments, but i can assure you that we will do everything we can to prevent counterfeit medicines from entering our markets and endangering people's health in the future.

the commission's vice-president mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the international labour organisation has adopted the ambitious maritime labour convention, which sets minimum standards for working conditions on board ships: employment conditions, housing conditions, social protection, not to mention the implementing provisions. the added value of this convention, which is a real draft of an international maritime labour code, is that it makes existing standards more effective, adapts them to globalisation and, above all, makes it possible to increase the number of ratifications by states. the commission, like the ilo, considers the objective of a level playing field to be fundamental. we are convinced that the maritime labour convention will help to do this, by eliminating shipping that does not meet minimum standards and making the seafarer's profession more attractive. however, the convention must be ratified quickly to produce its practical effects. a decision authorising member states to ratify the convention is legally necessary since the rules in force at the ilo do not allow the community as such to ratify the text, even if it contains provisions falling within community competence. in order not to delay the ratification procedures, the commission endeavoured to submit its proposal for a decision promptly after the adoption of the convention. in its proposal, the commission provides for the principle of the power to ratify and suggests 31 december 2008 as the deadline for depositing the instruments of ratification. the commission therefore wishes to maintain a firm wording on the commitment to ratify the convention and rejects drafting which would weaken this principle. i would like to thank you, mrs mcdonald, and i would like to give you my full support for your report which maintains the 2008 deadline. given the level of european standards, it is likely that third countries will be much more affected by the entry into force of the convention than member states, which already apply more stringent standards. the entry into force of the convention will therefore reduce the gap between the standards of most third countries and those of the community, which should favour fairer conditions of competition. entire parts of the convention are already covered by equivalent provisions in community law. this will avoid the need for member states to revise their legislation as a whole and will enable them to speed up ratification. the commission can understand the internal constraints of the states and, in this context, can be more flexible on the time limit itself, but not on the principle of a firm deadline without conditions. it would be a real pity to break the momentum we have had in the geneva negotiations by member of the commission. madam president, although votes have wings and they go from one party to another, i am more interested, not in the issue of votes, but in the issue of poaching. i think that the honourable members cannot possibly not know the answers to the questions they have already asked. they know that everything that has been agreed on the accession of countries to the european union is public. there are no secret agreements and i am sure that the honourable members are fully aware of this, because they have been in the european parliament for over two years now. so i can't quite figure out what these classified documents are. there's no secrecy here. everything that's been agreed is public. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the fisheries sector is not left behind. there is no agreement on anything else. as regards derogations, the right to request derogations is provided for in article 9 for all member states. malta may also request a derogation in accordance with the provisions of article 9. malta did not ask for a derogation, it simply made the derogation itself, we took it to the court and we have been waiting since july 2006 for a reply. he hasn't sent us a reply yet. the commission is particularly pleased with the active intervention of parliament's committee on petitions. the visit of the members of the committee on petitions to malta in may 2006 was fruitful and the report on the visit confirms that the views of the commission and the european parliament are in agreement on this matter. the commission used the infringement procedure because the maltese authorities continue to allow spring hunting in breach of community law. malta's criminal behaviour is obvious! it started with the 2004 hunting season but has continued in the years since and, it seems, is continuing this year. the commission considers it a priority to prevent systematic and widespread infringements of community legislation on birds. we therefore intend to extend the existing - as i said earlier - open infringement procedure, which concerns the 2004 case, to cover malta's generalised infringement practice. in this way we will be able to deal with and prevent future infringements, which will be done at the commission meeting on 21 march. as regards the present situation, a commission delegation will be visiting malta on 28, 29 and 30 march to discuss the matter in more detail. the competent national authorities will be asked for explanations and made aware of the need to comply with community legislation without delay. if the maltese authorities persist in their position, the commission will proceed to the next stage of the procedure, namely the adoption of a reasoned opinion, and may then immediately refer the matter to the court of justice. the procedure which the commission can follow - for any case, i am not just talking about malta! - in the main proceedings, and after issuing a reasoned opinion in accordance with article 228, to seek interim measures ordering the member state to bring the infringement to an end. the court may order interim measures if it considers that there is an urgent need to prevent irreparable damage resulting from a manifest and manifest breach of community law. in the case of malta, the commission could not have requested interim measures today if it had not previously extended - as i said before that it would - the scope of the 2004 case to cover subsequent years (2005, 2006 and possibly 2007). the court would have rejected the application, since the risk of irreparable damage would have already passed. the application for interim measures would be without purpose if it concerned only the 2004 infringement. it is for this very reason - from a legal point of view and in order to prevent future infringements - that the current procedure should be extended at the commission's meeting on 21 march. i hope that the visit of the directorate-general for the environment will convince the maltese authorities to comply fully with the provisions of community legislation.

member of the commission. mr president, honourable members, i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr schapira, for this report that brought due attention to the role of local authorities in development cooperation. the commission shares most of the rapporteur’s observations and agrees on the high importance of local authorities, both for better governance and for improving the wellbeing of populations, for example through better service delivery in the basic social sectors. the commission pays great attention to this aspect, on the one hand by supporting decentralisation processes and local governance through geographic and thematic instruments and, on the other, by involving local authorities in the programming process itself. while decentralisation is considered one of the important areas of cooperation under geographic programmes, the commission does not impose focal sectors on the partner countries. instead, focal sectors in each country are decided following the principle of ownership and in close consultation with all stakeholders. the commission’s delegations have been provided with guidelines on how to facilitate the inclusion of local authorities’ representatives in the whole consultative process. in cases when the government did not select specific support to local authorities as an area of cooperation, the latter were often supported through sector programmes – in health and education – or through other types of interventions, in particular defining decentralisation policy, elaborating a legal framework and/or supporting planning and financial management capacities at local level. another instrument at our disposal is the thematic programme, non-state actors and local authorities in development. it is designed to be subsidiary and complementary to intervention programmes in the country strategy papers. for the period 2007-2010 an amount of eur 903 million has been earmarked for this programme, of which up to 15% can be allocated to local authorities. as you know, mr president, it is an actor-oriented programme aimed at capacity-building through support to own initiatives from local authorities and non-state actors originating from the eu and partner countries. its main objectives concern the facilitation of local authorities’ and non-state actors’ participation in poverty reduction and sustainable development strategies as well as strengthening their networking activities. regarding the involvement of local authorities in creating development policies, efforts are being made both at global and country level. at global level, the commission has established continuous dialogue with the existing european and international platforms such as the united cities and local governments, the council of european municipalities and regions and the committee of the regions. at country level, the participation of local authorities in the programming process was introduced under the ninth european development fund. it then became an essential principle of the ongoing tenth edf programming process and, as i have already mentioned, the commission’s delegations are actively promoting this process. following the adoption of the final country strategy papers, the commission will draft a report to assess the progress made in promoting participatory approaches under the tenth edf. the analysis will examine a number of issues relating to the consultation process, including questions such as the one mentioned by the rapporteur, whether the consultations held with stakeholders were based on draft csps. we are all convinced that close cooperation with the local authorities can bring important benefits to our efforts to combat poverty in the world and i am confident that this process can be further improved through our joint efforts. the report we are discussing now is an important contribution to these efforts.

the agenda includes the debate on the report by mr adamou adamou, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and food safety, on halting biodiversity loss by 2010 (2006/2233 (ini)) (a6-0089/2007).
member of the commission. madam president, first of all i would like to apologise on behalf of commissioner dimas, who regrettably could not be here today. it was precisely one year ago that the commission adopted its communication on halting the loss of biodiversity by 2010 and beyond. given that tomorrow is international biodiversity day, it is a fitting time for parliament to debate its report. i am pleased that parliament is using this opportunity to send a clear message to the world on the importance of protecting the planet’s biodiversity. the theme of this year’s international biodiversity day is ‘biodiversity and climate change’. i have said before, and wish to underline today, that biodiversity loss is as great a threat to the planet as climate change. like climate change, biodiversity loss is an economic problem, a social problem and a growing threat to global security. both issues are closely linked. climate change is a major force behind species loss while at the same time the loss of ecosystems contributes to climate change. fighting climate change is now at the heart of the european project and is at the top of national political agendas. unfortunately, the same is not yet true for biodiversity loss. perhaps the threat is less apparent, but when we stop to look at the facts the situation is every bit as worrying. human activities mean that extinction rates are already between 100 and 1000 times the natural background rate – around 30 000 species a year, or three species every hour. if this process remains unchecked, we will have erased millions of years of evolution within the next few decades. this dramatic species loss matters because it weakens ecosystems of which species are the building blocks. the un’s 2005 millennium ecosystem assessment has two key messages. the first is that we are all ultimately dependent on ecosystem services, such as raw materials, medicines and clean water, for our prosperity and wellbeing. the second is that ecosystems are being fragmented, degraded and destroyed to the extent that some two thirds of the services that we receive from ecosystems are in decline. combined with environmental threats such as climate change, increasing population levels and increasing per capita consumption, this means the pressures on species and ecosystems are intensifying. without urgent action we will soon reach a point of dangerous and irreversible change in global ecosystems, just as without action we will soon reach a point of dangerous climate change. as with climate change, the window of opportunity to prevent dangerous ecosystem change is rapidly closing. last year’s biodiversity communication represents a first attempt by the european union to set out a coherent response to the problem of biodiversity loss. it should be seen as one of the most important policy documents issued by the barroso commission, and there are two innovations which are of particular significance. the first is that the communication introduces the concept of ecosystem services into the eu-level debate. it highlights the extent to which these services are essential to our prosperity and wellbeing and makes the vital link between biodiversity loss and the decline of those services. the second innovation is that the communication sets out a very specific action plan for the period 2007-2013. the action plan is an important step forward since it spells out what needs to be done both at community level and at member state level. it is only through complementary actions at these two levels that we will be able to make the necessary progress. the action plan also makes it clear what needs to be done to meet the european union’s commitments to halt the loss of biodiversity in the eu, and to reduce significantly the rate of loss worldwide, by 2010. with the inclusion of a process for regular evaluations against a clear set of targets, both the commission and the member states can be held to account on its delivery. i am very pleased to know that parliament’s report welcomes the communication and its action plan. i wish to thank the rapporteur mr adamou for his efforts, and mr berman and mr gklavakis from the committee on agriculture and rural development and the committee on fisheries respectively for their contributions. the report echoes the equally warm reactions of the council, the committee of the regions and the european economic and social committee, as well as that of environmental ngos. it seems we have a broad consensus on what needs to be done. the challenge now is changing this political support into real actions on the ground. there can scarcely be a more important question for any parliament to debate than the survival of life on earth. i urge you to use this opportunity to send a clear message on the gravity of biodiversity loss and the need for full and vigorous implementation at all levels of the biodiversity communication and its action plan.

madam president, access for exporters and businesses to the markets of many of the union's major trading partners is not always easy. it faces high tariff and technical barriers, opaque and unfair practices, administrative and fiscal obstacles and, more generally, the failure to fully apply the principle of national treatment. i also stress, as the rapporteur mr caspary has said, the ineffective protection of intellectual and industrial property worldwide. an additional factor in the reduced competitiveness of european products and services is the obligation to comply with stricter standards of product safety, protection of public health and the environment, consumers and workers. i am not in favour of relaxing the european regulatory framework, but of seeking reciprocal conditions with our trading partners. the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the community's financial instruments are used to finance the necessary measures to ensure that the community's financial instruments are used to finance the necessary measures. in this context, the european union is rightly seeking, in the context of the current wto negotiations, to achieve zero import duties on so-called 'green goods'. the commission will also consider the possibility of imposing a 'green tax' on imports from countries not bound by the kyoto protocol in order to compensate for the competitive disadvantage of european companies and to prevent them from relocating to areas with less stringent environmental rules. the balance of the world trade system requires converging systems, institutional transparency, converging standards of social and environmental protection.
mr president, there is no doubt that aid for trade is a very important initiative. it shall support the fullest and most effective integration of developing countries, in particular the least developed among them, into the multilateral trading system. as has been said, trade is not really a panacea for growth. it can, however, enhance the overall economic and social development of the recipient countries. the special and differential treatment of developing countries in the wto is to some extent mandatory, particularly as regards the least developed countries. it should be noted, however, that the adoption of multilateral commitments and their compliance with wto rules provide an incentive for reforms which will benefit the developing countries themselves. the gradual opening of their markets and their exogenous economic and trade policies help to strengthen their competitiveness by enabling the transfer of technology and know-how. developing countries, however, are particularly reluctant to negotiate multilaterally in calls for opening up their markets. to this end, trade assistance is crucial in order for these countries to meet new obligations and implement multilateral trade rules, mitigate their adjustment costs to reforms and integrate trade more effectively into their development policies. it is recognised that aid for trade should be accompanied by appropriate internal policies in developing countries in order to maximise the effect. and in this endeavour, the european union is called upon to play a leading role in shaping an effective, coherent, targeted aid agenda for trade. in conclusion, i would like to congratulate commissioner mandelson on his support for this initiative and also for the link between the external aspects of competitiveness and the internal initiatives for the competitiveness of the european economy which was the subject of the previous part of our debate.
in writing. the title on environmental quality standards in the field of water policy is substantially out of line with its content, since it focuses on harmful substances in surface water and sediments derived solely from herbicides. other sources of pollution are out of control, such as industrial liquid waste, urban sewage, landfill drainage, thermal pollution from similar sources, pollution of lakes by gaseous pollutants from combustion plants precipitated by weather phenomena, etc. however, chemical pollution of surface water can cause disturbances in aquatic ecosystems, destroying biodiversity or accumulating pollutants in the food chain from infected fish. the commission's intention to target and blame agricultural production as the sole responsible for the chemical pollution of surface waters is also clear. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the environment is protected, and that the environment is protected in all its aspects. no specific measures are proposed to control the sources of discharges of the priority substances, dangerous and non-hazardous, whose concentration limits are dealt with in the proposal for a directive. however, the report extends the limited scope of the directive to more effective protection of water. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the quality of water is not compromised by the lack of adequate protection of the environment, and that the quality of water is not compromised by the lack of adequate protection of the environment.
in writing. the much-touted improvement of agricultural production and the improvement of agricultural products through organic farming is in danger of becoming a colossal fraud on producers and consumers. the few multinationals that are trying to control the global food chain through mutants for their profits have been imposed with the responsibility of all the political groups in the ep including pasok-nd. the authorized presence of gmos and the addition of supplements (vitamins, etc.) derived from gmos to organic food is the back door to the use of gmos in countries and regions which resist their use by recognizing their dangers. the establishment of a limit for the detection of gmos in organic products, however low it may be, allows it to be increased without control, since even the european parliament has not been given the right to co-decide. the limit will now be set by multinationals in accordance with the natural contamination resulting from the permissible coexistence of conventional, genetically modified and organic crops, whatever protective measures are taken. so organic producers will see their products degraded while consumers will be cheated into buying 'organic' gmos. our proposals to ban gmos in organic food have unfortunately not been accepted, but the struggle continues with the workers for healthy crops and healthy food.
in writing. the eu's interest in halting biodiversity loss is late and hypocritical, because it does not take any substantive measures, nor does it have the necessary resources. at the same time as it appears to be cutting for biodiversity, it has as its basic hierarchy the promotion of gmos. the report correctly mentions the risks of genetically modified fish. it does not mention at all the enormous threat posed by resistant gm plants which reduce plant biodiversity and pose dangers to public health. there's already a wealth of evidence for a wave of species extinction, with loss rates 100 to 1,000 times higher than normal levels, with tragic consequences for the genetic flow between wildlife populations. climate change, environmental pollution, intensive agricultural production methods and the inadequate management of forest land and water resources are cited as the main causes of biodiversity loss. but these are the results of the predatory exploitation of nature by the monopolies for their profit. but the polluter pays principle also absolves the polluter, legitimises and markets environmental degradation for the benefit of capital profits. in essence, the responsibility of governments and the eu is being transferred to citizens, by strengthening education and awareness. the people should seek to hold the eu and the governments of the member states accountable for their anti-environmental policies, condemn them and overthrow them.

member of the commission. the honourable member asked me what i mean by the expression ‘our european way of separation’. we currently have a framework for telecoms that provide regulatory tools or remedies to the nras in cases where markets are not competitive, and in its review of the framework the commission will be looking at ways of strengthening the single market for telecom services. one possible innovation is to work more closely on remedies, because remedies are sometimes either not applied or not applied swiftly, which is the same problem. we have also analysed that one possible tool as a remedy could be functional separation, which means separating the network business of a dominant market player from the part of the business that provides a service to the end customers. this functional separation can provide the right incentive to providers of network services not to discriminate between customers for wholesale services. this can in turn mean that the conditions for real competition in the telecom markets are improved. so we are not speaking here about forcing dominant players to sell off part of their businesses, as has happened in other parts of the world – for example in the united states with at&t. we would not like to go in that direction, and that is why i am talking about ‘the european way’. it would then be for each national regulator to assess the condition in its own member state before considering such a remedy. this has already been done in britain with openreach, so that is one example which we have in that case. the honourable member also asked about greece. in the case of greece it would then be the greek regulator, on the basis of national law in line with the updated eu framework, to take account of competitive conditions and all other relevant factors in the greek market, and then to propose – or not – such a remedy if he thought it to be necessary and in the interests of the greek market.

i have to say that i am not in favour of this. madam president, allow me to wait two minutes for the commissioner to take his seat, and please do not count that time. the concept of decent work as a set of rules and conditions guaranteeing respect for the worker as a human person was introduced by the international labour organisation in 2000 and developed into an internationally pursued objective by the recommendations of the united nations conference of heads of state and government in september 2005 in the context of achieving the millennium development goals. in july 2006, the high-level ministerial working group of the united nations economic and social council underlined in its statement the need to give priority to efforts to achieve productive full employment and decent work for all. the concept, attributed to the latin-derived adjective decent, has the meaning of concession, of consent so that there is decency. the greek word ʽad·iʹdho·naiʹ emphasizes the need to assign value. the german adjective 'menschenwürdig' is, however, i would say, fully reflective of the aim of the global project, as it combines dignity with the human condition. the commission communication of may 2006 'promoting decent work for all' lays the foundations for the european union's organised contribution to the implementation of all the objectives of the integrated vision of human work in conditions of freedom, equality, safety and human dignity. the four main pillars of the concept of decent work are, as is well known, the creation of jobs for productive work with free choice, the guarantee of labour rights, extensive social protection and the provision of health and safety conditions, the promotion of social dialogue and the peaceful settlement of disputes along the lines of respect for equality between men and women. five ilo conventions enshrine basic labour rights: freedom of association, promotion of collective agreements, abolition of child labour and equal pay for men and women. we hope that the other ilo conventions still awaiting ratification will be signed and implemented. following the council decision of december 2006, the employment committee of the european parliament welcomes the commission's objectives in its report. the objectives must be:- to achieve social and economic progress and to ensure that it is equitably distributed for the benefit of all; - the promotion of entrepreneurship by adjusting expenditure to the changing phases of the business cycle; - the development of active labour market policies as a component of macroeconomic policy; - strengthening the institutional capacity of the social partners to participate and developing social dialogue; - enhancing the employability of all levels of workers, especially women, young people and older people, through renewed education systems; - consolidating lifelong learning so that all can benefit from advances in science, technology and communications and adapt to the increasing demands for qualifications and skills. there is certainly no single model of social policy and labour market regulation. the european union is proud that, in addition to the broad effort of its member states to ratify the ilo's international conventions, it is the economic power which, throughout its length and breadth, exhibits common features of social sensitivity. the european social model, with the aim of productivity and economic performance for the benefit of all, high-quality social benefits, health and safety conditions, care for training, education and retraining of all ages and categories of workers and social dialogue ensuring equal opportunities for all. the european employment strategy, the social protection and social inclusion strategies, the national reform programmes, the revised lisbon strategy for growth and employment with the preservation and improvement of the social acquis, the european sustainable development strategy, constitute the european union's roadmap for achieving the objectives of decent work. but decent work is also a matter of governance. the implementation of effective decent work policies requires accountable institutions, political commitment to sound state management and an active and organised civil society. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the european union is able to meet the challenges of the future. but economic globalisation, the globalisation of markets, technologies, information and labour is a phenomenon that is expected to accelerate with the strengthening of economic multipolarity. china is rising to the top, as are india and other powers. the gap between rich and poor is widening even in developed and industrialized countries. it is time for the european union to show the world its values. in this report, the european parliament reinforces the commission's intention to integrate decent work into its external policies, in cooperation with the un institutions, national and regional organisations, the social partners and other sectors of civil society. the commission and the member states are invited to coordinate decent work more effectively in external cooperation and trade policy programmes and to contribute to the implementation of the ilo national decent work programmes. i thank the three committees that have given their opinions and all those who have contributed to the presentation of this report.

in writing. the report uses the existing problem of organised crime as a pretext to promote a tougher policy of restricting fundamental individual rights and strengthening the police state and the unchecked action of eu law enforcement mechanisms. in this context, it proposes: the convergence of the criminal laws of the member states, paving the way for the 'communitisation' of criminal law, by limiting one of the most important foundations of the national sovereignty of the member states. the creation of joint investigative teams on law enforcement, the autonomy of europol and eurojust and the strengthening of their character and powers so that they can act as a 'driving force' in the conduct of member states' policy. recognising the fundamental role of the eu counter-terrorism coordinator, instituting a whistleblower mechanism, calling for 'the establishment of a regime of partners in the administration of justice at european level'. of course, after all this, it is not at all surprising that the report makes no mention of the interconnection of organized crime with state institutions, nor of the state's own repressive mechanisms, although their underground relations are a common secret. it is clear that the real aim of the report is to 'fight' democratic rights and civil liberties, not organised crime.

the president of the council. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. i thank you very much for inviting me to the house. the invitation comes at the right time. as you all know, we are still trying to get through a summit, namely the g8 summit in heiligendamm, but we are of course well aware that in about 14 days' time there will be a summit, an event - i am sure you will agree with me - which will be decisive for the future of europe. we hope that this is also well understood by all those involved in the european council. i - i can assure you - have never in my life had so many bilateral talks with our european partners and colleagues as in recent weeks, and others in the german government, including our chancellor, are doing the same. we have been celebrating 50 years of european unity in berlin, brussels and throughout europe for just two and a half months. the european union is a model of success. many people in the world - and i can say this as a foreign minister who travels frequently outside the european union - are envious of this model. i am not saying that the european union should be a political union, but that it should be a political union. as you know, the success goes far beyond that: we have open borders and a single market of 500 million people. the european union can point to the fact that disadvantaged regions in europe have achieved growth and prosperity. but we all know, of course, that this success is not automatic and that there is no guarantee of similar success in the next 50 years. that is why we knew on 25 march, the european birthday, what a difficult task we will have to face today, and especially at the european council. the aim is nothing less than to create the new foundations for the european union. it is a renewed treaty framework which will enable us to remain operational in the world of the 21st century in an enlarged union. the main theme of the forthcoming european council on 21 and 22 june will be to set the stage for the success of this treaty reform. the expectations of the summit are high and i think we would do well not to raise them any higher. never could the real reach the imagined: for to think of perfections is easy, to realize them is very difficult. so said balthasar gracián as early as the 17th century. we are doing well to approach the matter with realism in the european council. i am optimistic, however, because the eu has shown, especially in recent months, that it is capable of taking decisive action when its member states are ready to do so. i would remind you of the groundbreaking climate and energy decisions of last spring's summit, which, as the debate in heiligendamm shows, have become something of a benchmark for the entire international climate change debate. or think of two very recent european legislative projects: the roaming regulation and the creation of a common european payment area. i know that the european parliament was very much involved in both projects. concrete policies in the service of citizens, responsible and forward-looking external action - this is also part of the philosophy of the forthcoming european council, and i will say what we will be dealing with outside the main constitutional issue: for example, the efforts to establish a common integration policy. we have done well in seeking common solutions with the north african transit countries. but we also know that strengthening frontex and strengthening the coastguard of the north african states is not enough to create a migration policy. we need help for the transit countries and above all we need economic stabilization for the countries from which most refugees are coming to europe. the fact that the european ministers of the interior and of labour have now met for the first time to hold joint talks is very welcome. another area of justice and home affairs policy that is of particular concern to people in the new member states is the extension of freedom of movement within the eu. we therefore want to make preparations for the enlargement of the schengen area as quickly as possible, so that this enlargement can be completed in 2008. we will also present a report on the further development of the european neighbourhood policy at the european council. we have every interest - and colleagues share this - in linking our neighbours to the south and east as closely as possible to the european union. and we will do this through increased sectoral cooperation, for example in the energy sector, in the transport sector, through participation in the internal market, adoption of eu law and intensive exchanges in education and culture. there's a lot of work to be done. i am also glad that i have personally committed myself to the adoption of a new european union approach to central asia. this is a region which has not been so much in the spotlight of europe so far, but with which we must seek closer cooperation, and i stress this again, not only because of the economic opportunities that lie in this region, but also because this is a region which is highly affected by the instability on the southern borders, see afghanistan and iran, and because it is a region which stands for a moderate islam and therefore remains available to us as a partner. i am aware, of course, that the success of the european council does not depend decisively on the issues i have just briefly mentioned. all these issues are important, but of course the success or failure is measured by another issue, and that is the question of successful treaty reform within the european union. i am aware that the european parliament has given a great deal of support to the presidency on this issue. thank you for that. i had a brief look at the crespo-brok report yesterday and i think that in this report you have managed to maintain the difficult balance between the desire to achieve a good and ambitious result and the necessary realism, which i mentioned earlier and without which an agreement is not possible. you all know the initial situation. i found it in the report: 18 member states have ratified it. these 18 member states are no easier partners for us to talk to than those in a different situation in the ratification procedure. we know that there have been negative referendums, and behind parliament is also prepared to take account of these concerns. however, this too must be said in the light of the latest opinion polls. the people of europe are not against europe. on the contrary! they want a european union that is capable of action, that is efficient, that focuses on the essentials, that tackles problems and really solves them. i am convinced that the major european reform package with which we have entered the debate takes up many of the arguments which still form the basis of the criticism of the eu today, namely that the european union is too inefficient and too lazy in its decisions. i am therefore pleased that the talks i have had have shown that all the partners in europe are willing to implement the institutional reform package which i believe we urgently need, because they all know that only through institutional reform will we be able to make europe more democratic, more transparent and more capable of action. i have not seen anyone who thinks that renegotiating this institutional reform package will put us in a better position. i also had the impression that there was a general consensus on the policies. this concerns the european union's external relations, justice and home affairs, energy policy and the social dimension. there is broad agreement that we must preserve the progress we have made. the debate is whether we need to add to the substantive policies. i see a predominant willingness to add to the areas of climate protection and energy solidarity, both of which the european council has also said should be given special importance. i know you're looking with particular interest at that part of the bill of rights. the overwhelming majority - almost without exception - agree with us that we need to make the charter of vice-president of the commission. madam president, the next european council will be a very important test of the european union’s ability to deal with new and difficult challenges and to look ahead with ambition. the main issue, which will be the real test for the german presidency, is the treaty settlement, but the conclusions will touch on several other issues, and rightly so. it is important to show that the union is willing to deliver the right policies for its citizens directly and by creating an effective and democratic europe. this is all part of the same effort to move closer to citizens and to serve the common interest. mr steinmeier has given a comprehensive overview of the council agenda, so let me touch upon just three issues. first, migration: the increasing challenges and opportunities posed by international migration must be addressed in a spirit of true solidarity. recent events have underlined the importance of that. it means recognising that better coordination is needed to face up to the ever-increasing flows of migrants at our borders and in our seas but also to reap the benefits of migration for the labour market and for society at large. at the same time, illegal migration and trafficking in human beings are on the rise and require our immediate attention. the european council will be asked to apply a comprehensive approach to migration to the eu’s eastern and south-eastern neighbours. the european council should also pay attention to the need to further reinforce the management of our external borders. the rapid border intervention teams should become active very soon. secondly, the european council will return to the crucial issue of hiv/aids. the hiv/aids epidemic is a critically important public health issue for europe. we can only tackle it together by ensuring political leadership from the top and the involvement of civil society at all levels. it requires devoting attention to prevention, research, surveillance, treatment, care and support inside the union and in neighbouring countries. i would like to pay tribute to the german presidency for keeping this issue on the agenda, despite the fact that this is not often recognised in media reports about the council. thirdly, i would like to say a few words about climate change. it will not be at the core of the june summit agenda but, in the wake of the g8 meeting, it would be impossible for the european council to be silent on this issue. i want to assure this parliament that the commission is working very hard to meet the expectations of the european parliament and the european council and to maintain an ambitious and dynamic policy, both internationally and in the european union. specific legislative proposals will be adopted by the commission in the autumn and we intend to build on the european union’s credibility and leadership in fighting climate change. those are some of the key policy issues that will be covered by the european council. however, as we all know, the key issue will be to move forward to a treaty settlement. i need not repeat here the urgency of the matter or its significance for europe’s future. we discussed it here yesterday and our discussion on the brok and barón crespo report left no doubts about what is at stake. i believe that we can be cautiously optimistic about the results, even though i understand that we should perhaps not raise expectations even higher. the german presidency, as we have noted, has already made huge efforts over the last few months to build a new consensus among member states. the berlin declaration reminded us of what we were trying to achieve together, how much we have in common and how europe has made and will make a difference for the peoples of europe. since then, the presidency has been listening to the position of parliament, the commission and every member state. all have shown their willingness to find a solution to move europe forward. for the commission, the starting point for a new treaty settlement is clear. in terms of serving europe’s citizens, this discussion is not a theoretical institutional debate: the institutions are there to respond to citizens’ needs, to realise policy goals and to deliver results. they need the right way of working and the right standards of democracy, transparency and accountability. we cannot implement our agreed policies with one hand tied behind our back. we need the capacity to act in a changed environment in the europe of a globalised world. what does this mean for the european council? it means that we need a fair and balanced solution, able to command a true consensus. a second failure might have dramatic consequences for european construction. however, it also means maintaining a high level of ambition. a lowest common denominator solution might bring short-term harmony, but it could also store up problems for the future. simply introducing minor changes in the treaty of nice will not be sufficient. the commission welcomes the efforts to find a solution, and the first place to look for solutions is the constitutional treaty. regarding the substance, the major part of that work remains valid. the changes introduced by the constitutional treaty are still pertinent and they need to be translated into reality, not questioned. the community method must be protected, including the commission’s right of initiative. a single-pillar structure and a single legal personality would tangibly enhance the union’s capacity to speak with one voice and to act in a global world. parliament’s enhanced role and the advances in qualified majority voting should be preserved. as we see it, the constitutional treaty also brought a very good solution on how to involve national parliaments, one that strikes the right balance between the role of national parliaments and the role of the european parliament. similarly, we will defend the legally binding force of the charter of fundamental rights, which forms an integral part of the package agreed by the convention and the igc. we acknowledge that some changes must be made and we respect all those who have expressed their views in this regard. we will not run away from a serious discussion about the form of the text, the eu symbols or other areas that have been mentioned for discussion. as far as the form of the new text is concerned, we will do our utmost to ensure that any new text will be readable and accessible. our position in the negotiations will be ambitious and firm. let me also add a point that is closely linked to our debate on the treaty settlement. we do not just need a deal among the institutions and the member states; we are equally in need of a new narrative, a new way to explain to citizens what is at stake. we need to explain why the enlarged union needs a new treaty that provides more democracy, more coherence and a union strong enough to meet citizens’ expectations. europe’s citizens welcome the eu’s commitment to tackling today’s key policy challenges: climate change, migration, energy – the areas that mr steinmeier has already mentioned. this is what they expect, but we have not yet succeeded in persuading them to make the connection between effectiveness in these areas and an appropriate treaty settlement. all too often people still feel that the debate on the treaties and the constitution is the preserve of a rather small brussels clique. we need to show that it is a question of having the right tools to serve agreed political objectives. we need to continue to focus on debating the ways to achieve these objectives. parliament and the commission have made a major contribution together through the plan d strategy. if the reflection period is over, that does not mean that we should scale down our efforts to engage civil society and citizens in a debate about the future of europe. it will be of crucial importance in the european council, in an intergovernmental conference and in the ratification phase to show that a settlement is of real, direct benefit to citizens. i was happy to hear that most member states are clearly in agreement with the presidency’s approach for a short intergovernmental conference with a clear and precise mandate to negotiate a rather limited list of issues. as for the commission, we will be vigorously pursuing our role as the voice of the common european interest. the road to a treaty settlement has not always been easy, but we are hopefully back on track. if we can hold our nerve and stay focused on the needs of an effective and democratic europe, the result will give us a european union that can face the challenges of the 21st century with confidence. in writing. following the vote in favour of the prüm convention, an enhanced version of the schengen convention, the sis ii information system and the decision on the uncontrolled and unhindered collection and exchange of personal data - including those relating to political, ideological, philosophical and religious beliefs - the european parliament also approved the vis. this system, which legitimizes the collection, processing and exchange of personal and biometric data of all foreigners applying for visas to any eu country, to which the law enforcement and intelligence agencies of each member state have access, adds another link to the chain that the eu is looping around individual rights. the eu's ambition is 'to make the vis the largest biometric database in the world'! - what ? the european union has a duty to ensure that the european union is able to take action in the fight against terrorism, and that it is able to do so in a way that is compatible with the principles of the european union. the eu is increasingly becoming a stronghold for its own people and for citizens of third countries. but as capital intensifies the measures of repression and suffocating restriction of workers' rights to consolidate and secure its domination, so will the currents of resistance, disobedience, and inevitable struggle to overthrow the power of the monopolies and their reactionary union grow.
in writing. the european parliament gave its 'green light' today to incorporate the main provisions of the proms convention, known as schengen iii, into the so-called 'community acquis' and into the national legislation of the member states in a simplified way, i.e. without the signature and ratification procedures required for international treaties. these provisions oblige member states to set up dna files and allow law enforcement agencies to collect, store, process and automatically exchange dna data, fingerprints and other data and information even on persons suspected of committing criminal offences or of endangering public order and security. it provides that the purpose of exchanging such information is to safeguard public order in international mobilizations, in particular in view of eu summits. that is why it gives the right of joint operations and full powers, even the use of weapons, to foreign police authorities. the kke has denounced the further criminalisation of political and trade union activity, the preventive approach and the intensification of the preventive repression of popular movements promoted by the provisions of the treaty. the peoples must condemn this treaty, which is dangerous for individual rights and democratic freedoms, and must intensify their struggle against the intensification of authoritarian measures and the eu's anti-democratic and anti-people policy in general.
in writing. the kke votes against the report because, despite the improvements it proposes in the new version of the council framework decision, it accepts in essence its basic philosophy as a whole, which is the unlimited and practically uncontrollable ability of the eu's repressive mechanisms and the law enforcement authorities not only of its member states but also of third countries (such as the usa), even private individuals (!) to collect, process and exchange all the personal data of every eu citizen, including data concerning his political and trade union activity, his ideological, philosophical and religious beliefs! the target of repression is now every eu citizen, since it is allowed to collect and transfer personal data of any person without even being suspected of any act, simply for reasons of public order and security! the addition of 15 guiding principles for the protection of personal data is nothing more than a catalogue and an exposition of ideas, without any possibility of enforcing compliance with them by the law enforcement mechanisms. in fact, there is no protection at all, since exceptions to protection become the rule, simply and uncontrollably invoked on grounds of public security, while data protection is the exception, and almost impossible to enforce.
in writing. the proposed revision of the fruit and vegetables regulation is aimed at adapting it to the new cap, the eu's budgetary perspective and the wto. the decoupling of subsidies from production, the substantial reduction of community support and the abolition of the remaining traces of export subsidies will lead to an increase in imports and a reduction in exports, a shrinking of the manufacturing industry and the conversion of some factories into packaging plants for imported raw materials, a drastic reduction or even abandonment of some crops in which aid contributes a significant percentage of agricultural income. in greece the main victims will be the growers of juiced oranges, industrial tomatoes and raisins, products that are characteristic of the country. the result will be the concentration of fruit and vegetable production in a few hands, the massive uprooting of small and medium-sized farmers by means of decoupled subsidies, the increase in the profitability of the commercial manufacturers by ensuring cheap raw materials, both domestic and imported. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full, and i would like to thank the rapporteur for his report. the reluctance of farmers to join the cp is due to their role as intermediaries between farmers and the industrialists, in the interests of the industrialists. the kke meps are opposed to this and are voting against it because the proposed changes are another blow to small and mediumsized farmers.

member of the commission. mr president, the principal aims of the eu legislative framework are a high degree of protection of road traffic accident victims, the promotion of free circulation of vehicles and the encouragement of cross-border activities of insurance undertakings. the eu legal framework for compulsory motor insurance is a major eu success story. developed since the early 1970s, it has been a fundamental factor in making the free movement of motorists and their vehicles in the union a reality. the motor insurance directives have permitted the abolition of border checks on insurance, so the vehicles can be driven as easily between member states as between one country. they also allow for easy compensation for the thousands of accidents involving vehicles from more than one member state. the motor insurance directives require that insurers have a local presence for claims settlement and oblige them to be members of the local guarantee fund and the local green card bureau. this is to protect victims, in particular from having to enter into cross-border negotiations with an insurance company established in another member state. the membership of the local green card bureau ensures a smooth functioning of a system without a need to check the insurance certificates. all eu member states, switzerland, norway, iceland, croatia and andorra participate on the basis of the ‘multilateral agreement’. the link between the country where the vehicle is registered and the insurer’s membership of that country’s guarantee fund is also an expression of the solidarity of the local motoring population. european consumers have the possibility to seek motor insurance cover eu-wide as far as the above specific conditions set for insurers are met. whether insurers are prepared to enter into insurance contracts for cars registered in another country depends largely on the insurers’ commercial policy and their willingness to cover risks largely or wholly situated in another country, where the risk structures may be substantially different from what they are familiar with in their home country. with this in mind, it is perhaps not surprising that the volume of cross-frontier business in this branch is very limited. however, some argue that there is a lack of competition and that a higher volume of cross-frontier business might bring down motor insurance premium levels. we are assessing this question as part of our ongoing public consultation on retail financial services.

methodological changes communicated by greece. the committee also stressed the urgent need for greece to cooperate fully with eurostat and provide a fully revised inventory of its gdp and gnp, explaining in detail the new sources and methods used in the greek national accounts, in order to enable eurostat to carry out a full verification of the new data and to report the results of this verification to the committee. the revision of the inventory was submitted by greece to eurostat on 6 february this year in a 460-page document written in greek. eurostat, after the corresponding translation, is finalising the examination of this documentation and will send a mission to greece before the end of this month. this mission, like those carried out in other countries, involves experts from other member states in order to ensure the necessary degree of transparency. the results of the mission will be analysed with greece first and the comments made thereon will be taken into
