acting president of the council. as the honourable member will be aware, the european union has not currently agreed on any quantified target for investment in innovation. such a target would be almost impossible to define and implement, since innovation covers a wide range of activities that are very difficult to define and measure. the european union thus decided in 2002 to adopt an indicative quantitative target for r & d expenditure on research and technological development, called r & dt, i.e. the well-known barcelona target of 3%, since it is the r & dt actions internationally defined by the oecd frascati manual that are the easiest to measure and quantify. it should be noted that this objective has recently been taken as a desirable benchmark given the difficulties encountered in recent years in increasing private r & d effort in significant segments of the business sector. nevertheless, action to promote innovation and research is a very important priority in the european union's policy, and is carried out through various instruments such as the framework programme and the cip, i.e. the competitiveness and innovation framework programme, as well as through the structural funds. the seventh framework programme and the icp have been designed with the needs of smes in mind, the main beneficiaries of the icp, and the seventh framework programme introduced a minimum quota of 15% for the participation of small and medium-sized enterprises in research activities covered by the thematic priorities provided for in the specific programme 'cooperation'. it should be noted that support under the seventh framework programme for small and medium-sized enterprises can help to increase their competitiveness and their potential for innovation. mountain, island and very remote regions receive support from the structural funds and are also supported through the relevant thematic priorities of the 7th fp specific programme 'cooperation', in particular with regard to improving their transport, information, communications and energy supply situation. the research potential of the union's convergence and outermost regions should be unlocked under the specific programme 'capacities'. in addition to existing programmes and incentives, innovation will be further promoted by a number of initiatives currently under negotiation within the european parliament and the council such as the proposal to establish the european institute of innovation and technology, the eurostars initiative, actively involving innovative small and medium-sized enterprises and other initiatives under article 169 of the treaty and the joint technology initiatives provided for in article 171 thereof. in addition, the commission is currently preparing its proposal for a strategic action plan for set energy technologies based on a wide public consultation, which it intends to present before the end of 2007. in the same vein, i would also like to highlight the new approach to industrial policy in the context of sustainable development with a focus on climate change, in which innovation and the role of small and mediumsized enterprises in the european economy are key aspects. in all these initiatives, small and mediumsized enterprises will play a very important role, and some of them are also aimed at the particular interests of the regions mentioned by the honourable member, such as the 'bonus' initiative already planned, through which marine research in the baltic sea area should be coordinated. the portuguese presidency has been keen to pursue the 3% target for r & d expenditure, notably at the informal competitiveness council in lisbon in july, where the role of public and private investment in r & d and public policy measures that could also contribute to that target were discussed. the informal council to which i refer also dealt with the policy of small and mediumsized enterprises with particular emphasis on innovation and financing, internationalisation and energy efficiency. the portuguese presidency, by highlighting the role of the need for specific measures in the area of human resources in science and technology and the strengthening of measures in the area of the information society, also hopes to contribute to strengthening the conditions conducive to an increase in research and development and innovation efforts at european union level.

prejudiced in any way. concerning the question put by mr casaca concerning the ecosystem approach, i would like first of all to say that, yes, we in the directorate-general for fisheries and maritime affairs had commissioned a study by experts. it is a normal periodical exercise that we undertake, on how the common fisheries policy has operated, what the possible pitfalls are that have been encountered, in order that, from that exercise, we can learn from past experience and try to improve things. first of all, i have no problem with making this study available to the committee on fisheries. we know that it is very critical, but we accept that criticism because at the end of the day we are trying to implement the 2002 reforms of the common fisheries policy. we are still, in 2007, in the initial phases of real implementation of the 2002 reforms by moving in the direction of multiannual management and recovery plans, by moving in the direction of more ecosystem based management of fisheries. we have inherited a large number of years of management of fisheries, in a way whereby it was overtaken by the scientific advances, by the enormous increase in the number of vessels that went beyond any limits of capacity so to speak as a counter to what can sustainably be caught. and we have to see to it that we redress the situation and bring about a system of sustainable fisheries, measures and initiatives again which i hope will have the full backing of parliament: like a discards policy; measures and initiatives with regard to multiannual management of fisheries; management of fisheries by having more closed areas, closed seasons – these are all measures which go very much in the direction of the ecosystem approach to fisheries and the maximum sustainable yield. we have had the first example of a management plan on the basis of maximum sustainable yields in the plaice and sole management plan which was adopted in council only last june. so, we hope to continue moving in that direction in order to regain proper management of fisheries on the basis of the ecosystem approach. on the question put by mr morillon, i would like, first of all, vice-president of the commission. it has been drawn to the attention of the honourable member that the detailed answers provided below relate only to the commission, which is of course by far the major employer amongst european institutions. one of the purposes of directive 1999/70/ec concerning the framework agreement on fixed-term work is to establish a framework to prevent the abuse arising from the use of successive fixed-term employment contracts or relationships. to prevent abuse, clause 5(1) obliges member states, where there are no actual legal measures to prevent abuse, to introduce one or more of the following measures to prevent abuse arising from the use of successive fixed-term contracts:(a) objective reasons justifying the renewal of such contracts and relationships;(b) the maximum total duration of fixed-term contracts or relationships; (c) the number of renewals of such contracts or relationships. the rules governing the employment of staff in the european institutions are laid down in the staff regulations, which were discussed with staff representatives before being adopted by the council. the european institutions are thus bound by law to respect the provisions of these staff regulations. the staff regulations allow the european institutions to recruit three main types of staff: permanent officials, temporary agents and contract agents. temporary agents and permanent officials occupy a post in the establishment plan. there is no limit to the level of responsibility which permanent officials and temporary agents can exercise. the situation for contract agents is different. they do not occupy a post in the establishment plan and they must work under the supervision of a permanent official or a temporary agent. there are two distinct categories of contract agents. one category of contract agent was created to perform tasks which are non-core and which do not necessarily need to be performed by an official. such contract agents can be offered permanent contracts so their tasks can be considered as permanent in nature. the spirit of directive 1999/70/ec is followed for such staff as they are generally offered a first contract for a fixed term, an extension for a fixed term and a third contract for an indefinite period. in some cases a permanent contract can be offered directly upon recruitment. there are currently around 2 300 such contract agents working for the commission around the world, mainly in delegations, representations and administrative offices. a second category of contract agents exists to cover temporary or specialist needs not covered by existing posts, and to substitute staff temporarily absent, among others on maternity or parental leave. by limiting to three years the maximum total duration of successive, fixed-term employment contracts in any one institution, the staff regulations give de facto effect to clause 5(1)(b). such contract agents represent approximately 15% of the total staff. it is clear that permanent officials are the mainstay of the commission staff. contract agents provide valuable support on a temporary basis to the work of commission officials. there are currently around 3 200 such contract agents working for the commission in its different sites.

member of the commission. climate change is one of the greatest challenges of our time; it hardly needs restating here. it is not a trade issue first and foremost, but there are areas where trade can help. that is why the commission wants the doha round to deliver liberalisation of environmental goods and services and also sees scope for the new generation of free trade agreements to help facilitate sustainable trade. the commission is aiming to negotiate an ambitious and comprehensive post-2012 climate framework. if we succeed in including all major players, we will have gone some way, the furthest we could, to obtaining a level playing field for eu industry. that also means that the carbon leakage – the displacement of pollution from one place to another – that might otherwise flow from a failure to reach agreement will be avoided. our aim is to include all major polluters in a proportionate way and not to frighten away partners from the negotiating table in bali, and later on, by preparing trade measures for imports at this stage. we should rather address the free rider issue when, and only if, it actually arises. a well-designed trade policy can help the world deal with climate change by generating the wealth needed to pay for the mitigation and adaptation measures required. investment in trade, in both low-carbon goods and services, can carry skills and climate-friendly technology throughout the global economy, helping to address climate change at global level and in the most cost-efficient manner. throwing that away would be doing a disservice to climate change policy. it should not be forgotten that our approach to climate change policy has helped put european industry at the forefront when it comes to environmental low-carbon technology. the eu has a considerable first-mover advantage as a result. the stern report made clear that combating climate change makes economic sense, in addition to the numerous societal benefits, because the costs involved are lower than the costs of inaction. trade policy can support climate change objectives by minimising those costs and generating part of the finance required and by fostering regulatory frameworks that support investment and trade in low-carbon goods, services and technology.

member of the commission. i am not quite sure what the honourable member means by the ‘liberalisation of our trade policy’. by definition, trade can only take place when markets are opened and trade flows are, in effect, being liberalised. trade does not take place behind closed borders or where economies are being converted into fortresses, so of course the commission seeks to promote the liberalisation of trade. the global europe trade policy review and strategy that was presented and agreed by the commission and the member states a year ago sets out very clearly the interests of the european union, which are to maintain open markets at home, to promote and use multilateral and bilateral negotiations, to open markets abroad and to use effective trade defence measures to tackle unfair trade or unfair competition. those are the three legs of our strategy; each is equally important. the review of the third leg of that tripod is taking place after quite dramatic changes have taken place in the world economy, and indeed in the european economy, since the last review of our trade defence measures took place, which was over 10 years ago. we have a responsibility to make sure that our measures are operating as well as they could be and that they command consensus and support and solidarity amongst our member states. when that weakens, the trade defence measures become less easy or possible to use. it is in an effort to rebuild and restore that consensus, support and solidarity amongst our member states that we are undertaking this review.

in writing. the establishment of a european qualifications framework strengthens eu intervention in the education systems of the member states, the homogenisation and adaptation to predefined quality and efficiency indicators. it is another tool for substituting flexible 'learning' for education, outside the socially institutionalized process of education. the knowledge is replaced by a temporary, permanent training which will equip workers with the skills that capital needs every time. the recognition of these qualifications will not be based on the qualifications awarded by the official education system of each country, but on the basis of certification examinations in bodies controlled by employers. the disconnection between the degree and the possibility of pursuing a profession is thus further promoted. the link between different levels of education and different forms of learning, which is intended to equate experiential learning with systematic training, attempts to level labour rights and to reduce the wages of all workers to the lowest possible level. the general objective of the eu through the system of lifelong learning and the certification of vocational qualifications is to subordinate the whole of education to the priorities of the market and to the enhancement of the profitability of capital, in full proportion to the educational needs of workers and young people. the commission's proposal is not a good one, but it is a good one.
in writing. tax policy is a means of redistributing income in favour of capital. this is what all the centre-right and centre-left governments are doing and it is the direction of the eu of capital. the common tax policy is not a reality because of inter-imperialist contradictions. but even if there were, capital would serve its own profit at the expense of the people's incomes and needs. in its relentless competition, capital today moves easily and quickly from high-tax countries to lower-tax ones. however, in all member states the tax rate on business income is reduced, shifting taxes to personal income. the same is not true of the tax burden on labour income, which remains stable, while indirect taxes and vat have increased, widening inequality and the gap between rich and poor. this is also reflected in the oecd data, where indirect taxes in the form of vat reached 6,9% of gdp in 2006. the tax exemption of capital is thus systematically implemented and the tax burden of workers is increased by indirect taxes. this is also the case in greece, where the business tax has been reduced by 10 points, vat has been increased by one point and a further increase of two points is now being prepared. this is the capitalist barbarity that creates inequality and poverty for the many, this is what we must overturn.

the rapporteur. madam president, i should like to begin by paying tribute to the late mr correia, who made a major contribution to the drafting of a proper and comprehensive report, which was also mentioned by the vice-president of the commission. i would like to say that the subject we are discussing today has a very long history. it started with a council of europe convention in 1983. the convention has been accepted by all the member states. but that convention provided that the prisoner's consent was required for the transfer of the prisoner from one country to another. so that contract had no effect. a second convention was made, which provided that the consent of the prisoner was not required, but this convention was not signed by all the member states of the council of europe, and so that effort was also foiled. we are therefore faced with a new initiative by three member states of the european union, austria, finland and sweden, which have submitted a draft which was properly drawn up by the council and came as a framework convention. what does this framework decision provide for? it provides that a convicted national of a member state of the european union must be transferred to the member state of which he is a national or has his permanent residence or all his interests. this makes a lot of sense, because we see that it will be much easier to rehabilitate him when he gets out of prison, because when he is transferred to the member state of his nationality he will have much easier access to the language, he will have much easier access to his friends, his relatives and he will be in a familiar environment. this report, as you will recall, madam president, was voted by a large majority in parliament in june 2006. unfortunately, the bureaucratic approach of poland, which delayed the implementation of this framework decision by means of various procedural 'gimmicks', has been overruled, and we are now in the process of a renewed consultation. the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. it is not a european coincidence that each member state, for its own - insignificant - reasons, is undermining such a good measure. in such cases what kind of united europe are we talking about ? i would like to stress that, fortunately, the constitutional treaty presented by the portuguese prime minister the other day provides that there will be an increased majority in this area and that the veto will be finally abolished. i would like to conclude by thanking the vice-president of the commission, mr frattini, for his contribution and to wish him well, after 25 years, to see this right initiative become a reality as soon as possible.

the rapporteur. mr president, the number of non-attached members may be increased at any time by unforeseen events, depending on political cohesion within existing political groups or the possibility of reaching consensus among non-attached members, provided that the number necessary to form a political group is available. the provisions of the rules of procedure relating to the composition of the conference of presidents should therefore not, from the point of view of legislative policy, cover only the case where the number of non-attached members is small. parliament's rules of procedure are a set of rules with provisions - presumably of long-term effect - which must produce useful results not only for the time of adoption or amendment but also for future changing situations. for this reason, ad hoc situations which can change at any time, and even return to the status quo ante, must not lead to the adoption of new regulations every time. it is a question of parliamentary sovereignty, parliamentary autonomy, the ability of the house to organise itself, and i ask for a vote in favour.

vice-president of the commission. the new treaty, already agreed but not yet signed, does not include any general provision authorising the transmission of personal data of european citizens to third countries. in fact, article 15a of the new treaty guarantees the right, the general right, to the protection of personal data. article 24 refers to the application of this general right and the processing of data in the common foreign and security policy area. this means that the transfer of personal data to third countries is based on the general principles or relevant provisions of directive 95/46/ec on personal data, particularly articles 25 and 26. this personal data directive remains in force. according to article 25 of this particular directive, transfer of personal data is permitted only if the third country ensures an adequate level of protection. article 26 of the same directive provides for the strict and explicit conditions under which it is possible to transfer personal data to third countries in other cases. the framework decision on data protection in the field of judicial and police cooperation will also be another very helpful instrument. we made a promise. the promise is to adopt, in agreement with parliament, a framework decision on personal data protection by december. i am very confident that we will be able to get this very important political result. why? because the portuguese presidency seems very determined to reach this goal and there seems to be an overall consensus among member states. you perhaps know that we discussed the framework decision on data protection at the last formal justice and home affairs council. on this, of course, i warmly wish close cooperation with parliament, even closer than in the past, during the coming weeks. i think we have the common goal of getting it adopted before the end of december.

madam president, the subject of today's debate is mis- phrased. the success of the globalisation era is not in the european interest and the welfare of workers in the countries of the european union, but in the interest of capital. the new order of things shaped by the interests of business and multinationals in the context of globalisation - at community and international level - aims to increase the profits of capital through the intensification of the exploitation of workers. the statements made by mr sarkozy yesterday on globalisation confirm the european union's support for big business, underline the intensity of the inter-imperialist contradictions and the desire to use the european union as an aggressive bulwark against the other big imperialist centres and, above all, against the conquests and demands of the workers. the common denominator of all these pursuits is the full-frontal attack on the workers. reducing wages, increasing working time and adapting it to capital requirements, raising the retirement age, flexicurity and the restructuring of industrial relations are the main thrust of the lisbon strategy. we therefore consider that any cloak of globalisation cannot be used to judge the harsh reality experienced by millions of workers. the arguments put forward by the commission and the council on the protection of the environment are also not convincing.

the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work is a very good one. as a rule, globalisation is perceived by european citizens as an external phenomenon, i.e. without any significant european regulatory and political intervention. it is therefore the responsibility of the european system of action to demonstrate that it is indeed protecting a visible and measurable european interest while promoting global understanding. as regards the union's external trade agenda, i believe that priority should be given to ensuring reciprocal conditions of access to the market and equal conditions of competition, as the president of the french republic, mr sarkozy, emphasized yesterday. the strong european regulatory framework for environmental protection, consumer health and workers' health is an important indication of the union's political and institutional maturity. however, in order not to constitute a prolonged competitive disadvantage for the union, it should be met with an equivalent response from other leading international actors. synergy between the internal and external aspects of the lisbon strategy will help to promote the european model in the global governance arena. it is, however, affected by the reduced regulatory intensity and binding comprehensiveness of both the world trade organization and other international organizations. the union is called upon to play a leading and constructive role in increased international cooperation. it called for the adoption of binding commitments and international standards to promote regulatory convergence on an upward scale.

will not change the instrument as such, but it will of course be designed in such a way as to allow us to take due account of the experience of the last three years and to give greater weight to the issues that have come to the fore in the last three years. i would like to give you a few examples. we will have to put more emphasis on the link between competitiveness, energy and the environment. the question of how structural change is accompanied socially. and that seems to me to be the very big question in the debate today across all the groups. she's entitled to it. let me say something about that. i think it is a mistake to present investments in social stability and social security as gifts, as charities. on the contrary, they are also investments in economic efficiency. because it is quite clear that europe's economic performance is determined by the fact that we have a highly motivated, highly efficient workforce, and we have that because we have a high level of wages and a high level of social security. it is not that economic and social aspects are opposed to each other, but that, as has been said many times today, they complement and condition each other. i think that is a very important point. i would also point out that, in the light of the fact that we have a shortage of trained and qualified workers in an increasing number of regions and sectors, the question of employability needs to be addressed much more sharply than before. so i think we're in broad agreement on that. i would also like to point out that the commission also believes that the turbulence on the financial markets which we have recently experienced must be the occasion for international, multilateral action. we cannot simply let this go on, because it is, as has been said, an inherent structural defect in the international financial system. it is not a matter of individual failures on the part of the managers who are now being sent into the desert with compensation of between 100 and 200 million dollars, but it is a structural defect. i would like to make three very brief comments on the great debate which has taken place here today on the subject of globalisation. firstly, it is so difficult to find a common european policy in this debate because there is no agreement on what the european interest actually is. in our daily work we are constantly confronted with a very different definition of the european interest. depending on the situation, the european interest is low prices in the supermarket of one member country or a high level of employment in the industry of another. and that is a contradiction that cannot be resolved so easily. or a high level of employment in the steel industry in liège - a very recent example - or a high level of environmental standards in the european emissions trading system. we are constantly faced with these conflicts, and there is no common line between 27 member states on what is in the european interest. secondly, we cannot act as if we say that globalisation was good as long as it consisted of the domination of the poor countries of the south by the rich countries of the north. she was good for that long. and globalization is bad, where the countries of the south become competitors. i can't do that. and what is not possible is to approach the developing regions with the demand for high environmental and social standards, but not to be prepared to change our own policies. what i hear in europe today is that china, india, they need to change their environmental and social standards. that is true, but the chinese and the indians feel that this is pure european protectionism, because we have built our prosperity on using lower social standards and lower environmental standards, and now we tell the others that we want to keep what we have, but you cannot have it. this policy, ladies and gentlemen, is doomed to failure. i'll tell you what. the only thing that works is we have to demonstrate to these emerging economies that another way is possible. that it's possible to turn an ecological and social challenge into an economic opportunity. that is why we have an ecological industrial policy. i think we are largely in agreement on this point and, in the light of this, the commission will now work intensively to put forward proposals for the next lisbon cycle. they will then be dealt with by the spring council in march, so that the european parliament has ample opportunity to express its opinion on the concrete actions and proposals before the final decision is taken in march next year. member of the commission. mr president, i would like to thank the european parliament for the interest expressed in the cross-border management of music rights and the 2005 recommendation on online music. the commission’s 2005 online music recommendation aims to allow the music market in europe to develop in the digital environment. it aims to create a framework in which the best new online licensing model will emerge by agreement between the market players. this should allow authors, composers and music publishers to get a fair share of the distribution of their online works. the recommendation does not prescribe a particular eu licensing model, and leaves implementation of its principles to the market. exactly two years after adoption of the recommendation, the commission is assessing the development of online licensing practices in the music sector in europe. stakeholders were invited to comment on emerging online licensing trends by 1 july 2007. the commission received 88 replies from interested parties, such as collecting societies, authors, creators and music users in member states. the process of reviewing the submissions is still ongoing. only after a thorough examination will the commission assess further policy steps regarding the online operations of collecting societies. the submissions analysed so far show that most stakeholders do not see the need for a framework directive, and prefer market-based solutions to regulatory invervention. on the question of whether the 2005 recommendation is limited to online sales of some recordings, the commission would like to point out that the principles on transparency and governance set out in the recommendation should not be limited to online music sales and should apply to all the activities of collecting societies. to conclude, while the online market for music is still in flux, legislating in favour of a particular licensing model would appear premature. the commission will monitor developments and report back to parliament and the council as foreseen in the recommendation. any follow-up, if necessary, will be closely coordinated with the european parliament and the council.

clearly shows how much tourism is affected by different community policies, but above all how important this sector is for the whole of europe. tourism is an expression of the european way of life and well-being and at the same time an important economic sector with considerable potential for growth and employment. tourism already generates more than 10% of the european union's gdp indirectly and directly and accounts for about 12% of all jobs. but it is not only europe that wants to benefit from the extraordinary economic opportunities offered by the development of tourism. we must arm ourselves to compete with other traditional and new tourism markets. europe can build on competitive advantages that already make it a highly attractive tourist destination: we have an incomparable historical heritage; we have a unique geographical concentration of attractive and culturally diverse sites. and we have a well-deserved reputation for providing high-quality services. these are the assets we need to shape the future tourism product of europe. our destinations simply have to be the best and the most attractive. you must make an offer that will make europeans and non-europeans want to spend their holidays in europe - and do so again and again. this product should meet the same requirements as other products of our economy: it should be an innovative product, which is the best possible response to consumer needs; a product that meets the highest quality standards and is also as environmentally friendly as possible. in short, a product that reflects our european values and strengths. let me give you a few examples of how we promote cooperation and competitiveness in the tourism sector. last month we had the european tourism forum in portugal, an annual event that is a good basis for expansion. we are currently exploring other ways of enhancing europe's image as a tourist destination and hope to have your support. finally, let me stress that the promotion of sustainability in tourism is a central aspect of our policy. i am convinced that if we integrate sustainability into all areas of tourism, we will protect the very competitive advantages that make in writing. the resolution is dressed up in costless pro-environmental colours and general slogans to obscure the reactionary content of the imperialist associations and organisations. it opposes air and road transport as being more co2-intensive than maritime and rail transport, but says freedom of choice (from multinationals) is fundamental to world trade. it calls for the trading of greenhouse gases for transport, which has failed to reduce co2 emissions but has proved to be a profitable trading mechanism for capital. it supports the goals of international monopolies for bold financing through the 'clean development mechanism-cdm'. it reserved to the eib the role of environmental watchdog acting on advice from the oecd and the g8 and asked that future proposals be those dictated by the wto. the bottom line is that natural resources continue to be seized by multinationals, forests continue to be deforested, freshwater resources continue to be restricted and degraded, desertification continues, mutants spread, toxics pollute, war conflicts and imperialist interventions perpetuate, greenhouse gases accumulate, billions of people suffer from the exploitation and profiteering of capital, and the resolution offers cover and help. that is why the kke meps will vote against it.

member of the commission. the commission has no competence over the siting of power lines, which is decided exclusively by the member states authorities under the respective eu environmental law. the council recommendation of 12 july 1999 on the limitation of exposure of the general public to electromagnetic fields establishes a framework of minimum restrictions and reference levels, but the member states are responsible for the implementation of the measures. as far as the possible health effects of exposure to electromagnetic fields are concerned, the scientific committee on emerging and newly-identified health risks has recently adopted an opinion which provides an assessment of the state of scientific knowledge in this area. overhead power lines are often the most cost-efficient solution for long-distance transmission of over 50 km. underground cables are also a proven technology, but until now used more for short- to medium- distances, and this is more expensive as things stand. the construction of overhead electrical power lines with a voltage of 220 kw or more and a length of more than 15 km has to undergo an environmental impact assessment. furthermore, any plan or project for overhead electrical power lines that is likely to have a significant adverse effect on natura 2000 sites is subject to the procedural safeguards set out in article 6 of council directive 92/43/eec.
member of the commission. i will start my answer with undergrounding. up until now, undergrounding cable technology has been used only in limited cases, like madrid airport. in principle there is now no limitation on the length of the cabling itself. the question is the cost. that cost would normally be around three to five times higher than overhead lines, and, to date, it has not been used for the very reason that you have two options. in fact, it has only been used when overhead lines are impossible. there are some cases where municipalities are now considering the use of cables, which will be ground-breaking cases. however, it will mean more costs for the consumer. concerning scientific evidence on exposure of the general public to electromagnetic fields, there is a general limitation, there are the council recommendations that i mentioned dating from 12 july 1999, and there are minimum framework restrictions and reference levels. however, as concerns further scientific evidence on damage to health, i am not aware of a need to go beyond those safety recommendations originating in 1999. basically, overhead lines are still a viable option and i believe that the choice between overhead lines or cables is one that should be made according to the situation, if one considers that cabling is not without its difficulties too. one needs to be aware that a natura 2000 site may be involved or that there may be some impact on the environment. there is no solution that makes zero impact on the environment. at the same time, there are technology choices that could be proposed, and companies are aware of these.
member of the commission. funding from the commission to support the operation of european environmental ngos is provided through a programme that has existed since 1997. the legal basis for the current programme is the life+ regulation. the objective is to strengthen the participation of european ngos in the development and implementation of eu environmental policy. a large number of diverse ngos have been founded during the course of the programme. lists of operations and amounts are published on the dg environment website. time does not permit me to read them all out, but the list will be forwarded to the honourable member. there is no geographic differentiation in the programme, since it is targeted towards european and not national organisations. to be eligible, the organisations should pursue activities in at least three eu member states. but only one of the organisations consistently funded, the mediterranean information office for environment, culture and sustainable development, is based in greece. many of them have greek member organisations, for example, the european environmental bureau, europarc and international friends of nature. grants are awarded in a yearly call for proposals. applications are assessed against award criteria and the ngos that have the best potential to contribute to development and implementation of the eu environmental policy priorities are selected. monitoring and evaluation is ensured by the commission, based on reports submitted by the beneficiaries as well as an in-depth audit. in this process, the extent to which the organisation has fulfilled its work programme and contributed to eu policy development and implementation is assessed.

member of the commission. ensuring that member states correctly apply eu waste legislation and preventing illegal waste activities are among the commission’s top priorities. the proposed environmental crime directive will ensure that serious environmental offences are subject to effective criminal sanctions throughout the european union. all serious waste-related crimes, including the illegal treatment, transport, export and import of waste, are covered by the proposed directive. the environmental crime initiative is, however, far from being the only action taken by the commission in order to prevent waste crime. the commission is taking a number of specific actions in areas where waste crime is a serious problem for member states. this concerns, in particular, illegal landfills and illegal waste shipments, which are covered by important eu legislation. the commission takes early action in order to prevent negative environmental and health impacts as a result of waste activities. awareness events concerning landfills and waste shipments are organised where the risk is high. last year, 16 such events took place and, this year, another 10 events are planned. multilateral meetings are also regularly held with national authorities and stakeholders to tackle bad implementation of eu waste legislation. guidelines are continuously developed regarding key eu waste legislation, such as on waste shipments and targeting particular problematic waste schemes, for example, waste electrical and electronic equipment and light vehicles. focus on such guidelines will ensure that eu legislation is uniformly and correctly applied throughout the european union. it is of paramount importance to know what is going on in the member states and to verify compliance on the ground. the commission closely cooperates with the impel network regarding, for example, joint enforcement actions on waste shipments and inspections and monitoring of landfills. systematic failures by member states to respect eu waste legislation are continuously met by legal action from the commission, including the powerful threat of fines under the ec treaty. for example, in 2003 greece was fined eur 20 000 a day for tolerating an illegal landfill on the island of crete. currently, a large number of illegal landfills in many member states are being tackled by serious infringement actions launched by the commission. the commission is also encouraging member states to make use of funding opportunities at eu level and to ensure that the waste programme expenditure under the various instruments contributes to the improved implementation of waste legislation. the eu waste shipment regulation contains the basis for cooperation between member states to prevent illegal waste shipment. we are currently examining the need for further actions in order to strengthen the enforcement of eu waste legislation, including legally binding rules for inspections of waste shipments. specific criteria could possibly be defined in order to ensure sufficient quality and frequency of inspections.
member of the commission. as for fines imposed on the member states, i would mention that, for greece, the fine is per day, and per year it is quite substantial. in my opinion, in the case of member states’ failure to enforce legislation, we should follow the legal infringement procedures that we follow, and it is the court which decides on the fine. for companies, the fines are also imposed according to national legislation if this is violated. so it is up to the member states to really strengthen these fines, because, from the commission point of view, we do what is required and we cannot prescribe the fines for not implementing vigorously enough eu legislation. it should be addressed through the court, because that is the legal structure of the european union. if there is a need to strengthen the system of fines, we will definitely follow this advice very carefully, because, basically, fines should be imposed in a way that prevents violation of the law, not just so that companies can shrug them off or pass the cost on to consumers. but, in this area, i believe that everybody shares the same objective, so i believe that the level of fines imposed today is not an issue. the issue is that legislation is not implemented vigorously enough and inspections are not particularly frequent, and that requires that the commission should take additional steps to guide the member states to take stronger action on waste crimes.
member of the commission. we have legislation on waste shipment, so this means there is common ground, and there is additional cooperation on penal matters, because the issue goes beyond waste issues. there have been developments, and current legislative processes allow companies that illegally ship waste to be penalised. i do not think we have difficulties owing to a lack of appropriate legislation, but rather because that legislation is not implemented.
member of the commission. the verification of compliance with the requirements of directive 91/271/eec on urban waste-water treatment is a complex task as it implies the evaluation of data concerning thousands of agglomerations all over the european union. the commission’s services collect and assess all information available and focus on the data included in the national implementation reports. when their assessment shows that member states are not complying with their obligations under the directive, the commission initiates infringement procedures in accordance with article 226 of the ec treaty. given the thousands of agglomerations which have to be checked, the commission has privileged a horizontal approach. thus, instead of randomly starting individual infringement procedures for each agglomeration, the commission has initiated global cases addressing the situation per member state and per core obligation. greece is one of the member states which still face significant problems in properly implementing the directive. as regards agglomerations of more than 10 000 inhabitants, greece has designated 36 sensitive areas. out of the 18 agglomerations discharging into those areas, 14 comply with the requirements of the directive. however, the commission considers that 10 other water bodies should have been designated as sensitive areas. there is an ongoing infringement procedure at this stage of a reasoned opinion. the greek authorities contest the need for the designation of those areas as sensitive. the assessment of the information sent is ongoing and, if necessary, the commission will not hesitate to bring the case before the court. as regards the specific question of the agglomeration of thriasio pedio, in its judgment of 24 june 2004, the court of justice declared that greece had failed to install a collecting system and to provide for appropriate treatment. the commission has therefore initiated an infringement procedure in accordance with article 228 of the treaty. the greek authorities have approved the construction of infrastructure required, which is co-funded by the cohesion fund. according to the information available, the project is planned to be operational by the end of 2009. as regards agglomerations of more than 15 000 inhabitants or their equivalent, out of the 75 agglomerations, 52 meet the standards laid down by the directive as regards collection systems for urban waste water and secondary treatment. with regard to the agglomerations that are not in compliance, the commission initiated an infringement procedure. in its judgment of 25 october 2007, the court ruled that 23 agglomerations still did not comply with the requirements of the directive. the commission has requested information from the greek authorities on the measures they plan to take in order to comply with the judgment. as regards the point raised on the reduction of the size of agglomerations, the commission verifies the information available and addresses any inconsistency in the framework of the ongoing infringement procedure. it should be stressed that, in order to comply, greece uses the european community funding available. as far as the cohesion fund is concerned, in greece 41 projects are currently open. the absorption rate is 49%. very often, such projects are combined projects which, apart from waste-water- and rainwater-related infrastructure, may also include water supply infrastructure. the erdf operational programme ‘environment’ co-finances nine waste water projects. these projects relate to the construction and/or modernisation of waste-water treatment plants and sewage networks. the absorption rate is 19%. as regards asserting regional operational programmes of the erdf, the question of absorption rates for the waste-water sector should be addressed to the competent regional authorities. contrary to the case of the operational programme ‘environment’, a member state is not required to inform the commission of the progress of each individual project.

member of the commission. mr president, a few points. first of all regarding russia, a point raised by various members. i would like to begin by saying that the community civil protection mechanism can be activated only upon a request by an affected country. official letters offering assistance were sent both to ukraine and the russian federation and, while ukraine answered positively, requesting assistance, russia declined the offer. but on the general issue of maritime safety, my colleague vice-president barrot wrote on 10 december to his colleague mr levitin, who is the russian minister of transport, to raise these concerns and to stress the importance of strengthened eu-russia cooperation in the black sea as well as the baltic sea – in order to improve maritime safety. addressing maritime environment problems at regional level is one of the cornerstones of the european union’s marine strategy and the proposed marine strategy directive, for which a second reading agreement between the council and parliament has been reached. i think this is a very positive development. the commission has set out its views on a strategy in the region in its communication ‘black sea synergy – a new regional cooperation initiative’. the proposal puts forward an initiative that would focus political attention at the regional level. the recent accidents in the black sea have notably involved a special category of vessels, the so-called sea/river oil tankers, which can only sail in open seas under certain restrictions. more generally the commission is concerned by the possibility that this category of vessels will trade in other sea areas of the european union or neighbouring the european union, and in particular the baltic sea. within the eu we have strict rules on maritime safety and the condition of the vessels, but we are also concerned about what happens in international waters both because it could easily affect the european union and because we are concerned about the global environment. that is why these accidents also demonstrate the importance of maintaining pressure on maritime safety issues both at eu and at international level. in this respect, as pointed out by parliament and by members already, it is important that examination of the seven proposals of the third maritime safety package is accelerated. finally, on the issue of response, the commission is also committed to continually strengthening the community response instruments, such as the civil protection mechanism, to ensure a rapid and effective response should such disasters occur again in the future. this also involves cooperation with the eu’s neighbours such as the black sea countries and of course other third countries. i would like to thank members for the debate and of course i will talk to my colleague about the interesting points you have made.
the agenda includes the debate on the report by christian ehler, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs, on deposit guarantee schemes (2007/2199 (ini)) (a6-0448/2007).
member of the commission. madam president, i wish to thank members for their contributions. in closing, i would like to make two key points. we do not believe that regulatory change is appropriate at the current time. the directive has stood the test of time well. it is able to adapt to changing circumstances. in the longer term it will be crucial from a financial stability perspective for the positive guarantee schemes to contribute to smooth crisis management in an increasingly pan-european banking environment. any further steps towards more harmonised schemes in the european union now depend therefore on the outcome of the wider work that is currently being conducted in the context of crisis management. concerning the problems raised by both ms kauppi and mr hökmark, the reimbursement of contributions to a bank that leaves the scheme, for whatever reason, is not covered by the existing directive and is therefore a matter for member state legislation. harmonisation at european level would require full harmonisation of the funding method. i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr ehler, and the committee on economic and monetary affairs, for their very constructive approach.
the debate is closed. the vote will take place on thursday 13 december 2007.

member of the commission. madam president, parliament’s report shows that both our institutions’ approaches to moving forward in the area of asset management are very much aligned. we also need future decisions to be based on a thorough analysis of impacts. we both want efficient markets that respond to the needs and expectations of the european fund industry and european investors. important efforts have been made in that direction. more important efforts are ahead of us. we are committed to delivering, but we should be cautious. we need to preserve the reforms and the repute of the ucits brand. we need to take the time to involve and consult with all stakeholders, and we need to avoid unnecessary intervention that risks distorting the market but does not bring about noticeable benefits. only when all those conditions are met can we be confident that our decisions are up to the challenge. we look forward to further cooperation between our institutions in this very important area.

the agenda includes the debate on the report by genowefa grabowska, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, on the proposal for a council regulation on jurisdiction, applicable law, recognition and enforcement of judgments and cooperation in matters relating to maintenance obligations (com ((2005) 0649 - c6-0079/2006 - 2005/0259 ((cns)) (a6-0468/2007).
mr president, as the european union, we are called upon to re-formulate - even now - our strategy for the important textile and clothing sector. the guidelines for an overall european strategy could be formulated as follows: first, to ensure improved access for european products to foreign markets, through the maximum possible convergence on a global scale of low-level tariffs and the elimination of non-tariff barriers. secondly, to ensure that the rules of origin are applied effectively to imports. thirdly, to give substantial support, through the globalisation adjustment fund, to smes affected by liberalisation. i also think it would be useful to set up a community programme to support the sector, particularly in the most disadvantaged regions of the union. fourthly, to ensure that the phenomena of piracy and counterfeiting are effectively tackled, given that the textile and clothing sector accounts for more than 50% of the cases recorded. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's trade policy is not distorted by unfair practices. sixthly, to guarantee that products imported into the european union are subject to the same safety and consumer protection rules. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. in any case, we ask the commission, that is to say you, commissioner mandelson, to apply this system strictly and effectively. i would also like to remind you of the ultimum remedium of the safeguard measures which the european union is entitled to take. in conclusion, mr president, the liberalization of the world trade system does not mean tolerating unfair competition, illegal trade practices and, ultimately, the deregulation of the economic and social model.
mr president, in europe, and particularly in greece, the textile industry is made up mainly of small and mediumsized enterprises. many of these businesses are located in the periphery. as the european union, we have an obligation to ensure the viability of the industry within our borders and to guarantee the protection of our businesses from unfair competition and illegal trade. the european textile industry must become more competitive at international level. we need to support measures to modernise our businesses, innovation, research and development. of course, we should be gravely concerned that the transitional period on restrictions on imports of textile products from china expires on 1 january 2008. but in a more general context and for the benefit of european consumers, we must also ensure the application of binding rules on the indication of origin of textile products and the effective application of the system of surveillance of imports from third countries.
the agenda includes the debate on the six motions for resolutions on eastern chad.
mr. mazzaki, we will all respect the time we know we have been allotted.

vice-president of the commission. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. the commission is deeply concerned at the deteriorating security situation in eastern chad and strongly supports the deployment of eufor forces in full force to protect refugees and displaced persons in the region. the european union will use all the instruments at its disposal in eastern chad to this end. the commission will provide more than eur 50 million, not only for eufor troops, but also as part of a comprehensive approach. this appropriation is intended to finance measures in the following three key areas, ranging from immediate aid to long-term development assistance. the first area concerns humanitarian aid, for which echo has already provided eur 30.5 million in 2007 in the form of emergency aid in chad to support refugees and displaced persons in various sectors. a similar amount is also earmarked for 2008 to continue these measures. the second area involves the establishment of a chadian police force to be tasked with humanitarian protection. in the context of the eu and un missions in chad, the united nations will recruit, train and equip up to 850 chadian police and gendarmerie personnel to be deployed in the refugee camps in eastern chad. the european union is supporting this un programme with eur 10 million from the stability instrument. the third area concerns reintegration and rehabilitation. in 2008, the commission will provide eur 10.1 million from the 9th european development fund for development actions to support reconstruction, conflict resolution and administrative capacity building. these are measures necessary to improve the security situation in the areas of the un/eu mission. the 10th european development fund provides for further measures, with a budget of eur 311 million for the period 2008-13. in the short term, these measures are intended to help the displaced return to their homes, and in the long term they are aimed at achieving a lasting stabilisation of the situation in chad and in the region as a whole. my predecessors have rightly pointed to the recent outbreak of fighting between anti-government rebels and president idriss déby's troops in eastern chad, which has made humanitarian aid delivery very difficult. the security situation in the areas surrounding the refugee camps is no longer guaranteed. the humanitarian situation is further exacerbated by the rapidly increasing number of refugees from the war zones. in this deeply worrying situation, the task of restoring security in the region is of the utmost urgency. to accomplish this task, a military presence is essential. eufor troops should therefore be sent to these crisis areas. but they will only succeed if the causes of conflict are removed and if at the same time a political process is initiated aimed at reducing underlying tensions and reducing poverty by promoting economic development.
the debate is closed. the vote will take place today after all the debates have been concluded.
the agenda includes the debate on the six motions for resolutions on women's rights in saudi arabia.
vice-president of the commission. the commission has already made a number of proposals. the commission is extremely grateful for the opportunity to speak today on the situation of women's rights in saudi arabia. the case which is the basis of your resolution gives us cause for great concern: a young woman was sentenced to 200 lashes and six months' imprisonment after being gang raped by seven men. the eu acted immediately on this matter. the eu troika made a demarche to the saudi government in riyadh, expressing the eu's dismay at the verdict of the court in el katif. the judgment is not only in clear violation of saudi arabia's international obligations, in particular the convention against torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. this verdict turns the guilt principle on its head by declaring the victim guilty. this case brings to the forefront a country where discrimination against women is unfortunately a daily occurrence. the european parliament has rightly called on the saudi government on several occasions to lift restrictions on women's freedom of movement, including the ban on women driving. this requirement also applies to restrictions on women's access to employment and to restrictions on their legal personality and representation in legal proceedings. i fully share the concern of parliament about the situation of women in saudi arabia. at the same time, saudi arabia, as a member of the united nations human rights council, is committed to the protection and promotion of human rights. saudi arabia is a party to the un convention on the elimination of all forms of discrimination against women. however, it has ratified the convention with one reservation; the kingdom of saudi arabia is not obliged to comply with any provisions of the convention which are contrary to islamic law in the event of a conflict between the provisions of the convention and the norms of islamic law. the european union has repeatedly called on saudi arabia to lift its reservations to this un convention, in particular with regard to the granting of equal rights for women and men with regard to the nationality of their children, and will continue to do so. human rights issues such as the situation of women are regularly the subject of european union demarches towards saudi arabia. the european union calls on the government of the democratic republic of the congo to take all necessary measures to ensure that the rights of women and girls are respected and that the rights of women and girls are protected. two recent changes we have observed could - i say this with caution - could perhaps point to some progress for saudi arabia. the national society for human rights in saudi arabia, for example, released its first report on the human rights situation in saudi arabia in may this year. the report reveals violations of the rights of women, prisoners and workers, as well as unfair court judgments. the findings and recommendations of this report should be taken up and followed up by the saudi government. in addition, in october, king abdullah announced a major judicial reform aimed at strengthening the independence of judges and facilitating the establishment of facts under sharia law under the supervision of the supreme court. for a country like saudi arabia, these are encouraging steps. we should therefore not only draw attention to human rights violations in saudi arabia whenever necessary, but we should also expressly welcome and support the reforms that have been slowly emerging recently.
the debate is closed. the vote will take place today after all the debates have been concluded.
the agenda includes the debate on the five motions for resolutions on the subject of 'justice for women in leisure'.
vice-president of the commission. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your kind words. in 1993, then japanese government spokesman yohei kono expressed "japan's sincere apology and regret" to all those "who have suffered immense suffering and incurable physical and psychological injuries as comfort women". in 1995, then prime minister murayama publicly apologized to the so-called comfort women on the occasion of the 50th anniversary of the end of world war ii. in the same year, the asian women's fund was also established to provide compensation and medical assistance to survivors on behalf of the government and the people of japan. these attempts to make amends to the so-called comfort women and the new public apology by former japanese prime minister koizumi on the occasion of the 60th anniversary of the end of world war ii in 2005 are positive steps by japan. japan has thus accepted responsibility for these unspeakable human rights violations. the japanese foreign minister has just confirmed the statement by mr kono, the government spokesman, which i quoted at the beginning, as the official position of japan. now we have the moving testimony of survivors, and this moving testimony has sparked renewed interest in this terrible time in europe as well as in the united states, canada and australia. but what we have to do here is not just to look back at the past, but to draw the right conclusions from what has happened and to do everything we can to combat the present forms of slavery, sexual exploitation and human trafficking. the european instrument for democracy and human rights is used by the commission to actively support non-governmental organisations around the world that work to prevent violence against women and children and to combat trafficking in human beings for the purpose of sexual exploitation. on 23 november 2007, the international day for the elimination of violence against women, the commission made another sign by reaffirming its commitment to combating gender-based violence. the european union has a regular human rights dialogue with japan, which addresses all eu concerns, including women's rights. japan is a like-minded global actor, working constructively with us in multilateral fora to improve respect for and protection of human rights. for example, japan has submitted a joint motion with the european union on human rights in north korea, condemning the actions of the myanmar regime.
the debate is closed. the vote on these three items will take place at the end of our sitting today.
